name: NJ-12
label: Safe D

key_factors: D+13 partisan lean gives Democrats a strong structural advantage
Hamawy's roughly 20-to-1 fundraising edge plus outside support versus Mele
Prediction markets price the Democrat near 98%
Open seat and no public polling add uncertainty
model.rationale: The district's D+13 lean, Adam Hamawy's dominant fundraising and outside-spending advantage over Gregg Mele, and markets pricing the Democrat at about 98% all point to a comfortable Democratic hold despite the open seat.
model.watch: Any late Republican advertising surge or independent polling showing the race inside single digits would warrant revisiting the forecast.
notes: No expert rater lists this race; treated as safe for the party holding the seat.
No usable general-election polls; forecast rests on fundamentals and expert ratings.
Open seat: Bonnie Watson Coleman (D) is not on the ballot.

overview:
New Jersey's 12th District is a Democratic-leaning open seat now that six-term incumbent Bonnie Watson Coleman is retiring. The district's roughly 13-point Democratic partisan lean gives the party a strong structural advantage, and no expert raters flag the race as competitive. Prediction markets price the Democratic nominee at about 98 percent to win.

Democrat Adam Hamawy has raised about $1.9 million and benefits from roughly $1.9 million in outside support, while Republican Gregg Mele has raised under $100,000 with about $10,000 on hand. No independent general-election polls are available, so the forecast rests on district fundamentals and the spending gap. The expected margin is about 21 points Democratic, with elevated uncertainty because polling is absent. A Green candidate and an independent are on the ballot but lack visible resources.
